Pre-election thread: what we know vs. what we don't (as of Oct 24, on current info)

KNOWN
- Election day is Mon Oct 26, polls open 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET. Mail-in ballots were due Oct 14 at noon.
- Simple plurality. No runoff and no ranked ballot. Alexander withdrew Oct 6 but is still on the ballot.
- Recent polls: Mainstreet (Oct 16-18) Bradford 48.9, Chow 47.5. Build Canada (Oct 11-16) Bradford 48, Chow 44. Pollara for CUPE 416 (Oct 13-19) Chow 53, Bradford 46.
- The "60% worried about privatization" figure comes from a poll commissioned by the water workers' union. It measures worry in connection with the plan. It does not show that 60% of all Torontonians hold that view.

UNKNOWN
- Turnout. The 2022 general had 563,124 votes and the 2023 by-election had 725,333. Which electorate shows up matters a lot.
- How Alexander's former supporters split.
- Whether sponsor and mode differences explain the poll gap. Probably partly, but I can't separate them.
- The fielding details of the union poll, which haven't been widely published.

A reminder: a 1-4 point lead is within normal polling error, and a recount is automatic only in a tie under the Municipal Elections Act. Otherwise it takes a council or board resolution or a court order. Market resolution should follow credible reporting and official City data. Treat any single poll with caution.

Base rates matter.

comments.name: 15 councillors
comments.content: A note from the councillor coalition. We don't endorse mayoral candidates. We also try not to amplify polling we can't verify. This Pollara release was commissioned by a union, which is an interested party. It is one of six public polls since Oct. 11, and they point in different directions. Could you share the sample size, field dates and how already-voted respondents were counted? Residents can then judge it for themselves. Whatever the poll says, please vote Monday, and ask every candidate where they stand on keeping Toronto Water accountable to Council.

comments.name: Quito Maggi
comments.content: Solid thread. The turnout point is the big one. The 2022 general and the 2023 by-election drew very different electorates, and each pollster's likely-voter screen is basically a bet on which one shows up Monday. That's where the polls diverge. IVR, online and hybrid will each get graded on it. Whatever happens, we'll all show our work afterward. Now get out and vote!

comments.name: User
comments.content: Good methodology detail. One note on reading these together: Nanos has Chow +3.2 (n=762, ±3.6, 16% undecided of all respondents). Liaison has Bradford +2 (n=1,000, ±3.1). Both are within the margin, but they lean in opposite directions, which is what you'd expect if the true gap is near zero. The Nanos undecided share matters more than the topline. A 16% pool is larger than either gap. So on current info I'd call it roughly 50/50, and I'd treat anyone claiming certainty with suspicion. Base rates matter.
